title: Photosynthesis
summary: How photosynthesis turns light energy into chemical energy in carbon compounds, how pigments and limiting factors are investigated, and (HL) how the light-dependent reactions and Calvin cycle work together.

keyterms.definition: Transformation of light energy into chemical energy when carbon dioxide is converted to carbon compounds, using hydrogen from water and releasing oxygen.
Splitting of water using light energy, releasing oxygen as a by-product and supplying electrons and protons (hydrogen).
A molecule, such as chlorophyll or a carotenoid, that absorbs specific wavelengths of light, causing electrons to become excited.
Distance moved by a pigment divided by distance moved by the solvent front in chromatography; used to identify pigments.
A graph showing the percentage of light absorbed by a pigment at each wavelength.
A graph showing the rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength of light, measured by oxygen production or carbon dioxide consumption.
The factor (light intensity, CO2 concentration or temperature) furthest from its optimum, which limits the rate of photosynthesis.
Free-air carbon dioxide enrichment: raising CO2 concentration around plants growing in natural ecosystems to predict future photosynthesis and growth.
An array of pigment molecules in a membrane that channels absorbed energy to a special chlorophyll pair at the reaction centre, which emits an excited electron.
ATP production in thylakoids by chemiosmosis, using a proton gradient generated by electron flow; can be cyclic (PSI only) or non-cyclic (PSII and PSI).
The enzyme in the stroma that fixes carbon dioxide by combining it with RuBP; the most abundant enzyme on Earth.
Ribulose bisphosphate: the 5-carbon acceptor of carbon dioxide in the Calvin cycle, regenerated from triose phosphate using ATP.
A 3-carbon sugar phosphate formed by reducing glycerate 3-phosphate using reduced NADP and ATP; used to make carbohydrates and other compounds.
The light-independent reactions in the stroma: carbon fixation by rubisco, reduction of glycerate 3-phosphate to triose phosphate, and regeneration of RuBP.

questions.prompt: Which energy transformation occurs in photosynthesis?
options: Chemical energy to light energy
Light energy to chemical energy in carbon compounds
Heat energy to light energy
Chemical energy to heat energy
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis traps light energy as chemical energy in carbon compounds, which supply most of the energy for life processes in ecosystems.
Carbon dioxide and water are converted to glucose, and oxygen is released as a by-product.

questions.statement: The oxygen released in photosynthesis comes from carbon dioxide.
questions.explanation: The oxygen comes from splitting water (photolysis). Water supplies the hydrogen used to convert CO2 into glucose; oxygen is the by-product.

questions.prompt: In a chromatogram, a pigment spot moved 3.6 cm and the solvent front moved 8.0 cm. What is its Rf value?
questions.explanation: Rf = distance moved by pigment ÷ distance moved by solvent = 3.6 ÷ 8.0 = 0.45. Rf values are always between 0 and 1.

questions.prompt: Why do leaves containing chlorophyll appear green?
options: Chlorophyll absorbs mainly red and blue light and reflects green light
Chlorophyll absorbs mainly green light
Chlorophyll emits green light during photosynthesis
Chlorophyll absorbs all wavelengths equally
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue wavelengths most strongly, which excites its electrons. Green light is mostly reflected or transmitted, so leaves look green.

questions.statement: An action spectrum shows the rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength of light.
questions.explanation: An action spectrum plots the rate of photosynthesis (e.g. O2 production) against wavelength, whereas an absorption spectrum plots the light absorbed by pigments.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its description.

pairs.right: Percentage of light absorbed at each wavelength
Rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength
Pigment distance divided by solvent front distance

questions.explanation: Chromatography separates pigments, which are identified using Rf values; absorption spectra describe pigments, while action spectra describe photosynthesis itself.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of paper or thin-layer chromatography of leaf pigments in order.
items: Grind leaf with a solvent to extract the pigments
Spot the extract repeatedly on a pencil origin line
Stand the strip in solvent with the origin above the solvent level
Remove the strip before the solvent reaches the top and mark the solvent front
Measure distances and calculate Rf values
questions.explanation: The origin must be above the solvent so pigments are not washed off; different pigments travel different distances, so their Rf values can be used to identify them.

questions.text: Oxygen is released as a by-product of photosynthesis by plants, algae and ___.
questions.explanation: Plants, eukaryotic algae and cyanobacteria all split water in photosynthesis and release oxygen. Fungi and yeast are heterotrophs.

questions.prompt: Why does the action spectrum of photosynthesis closely resemble the absorption spectrum of photosynthetic pigments?
options: Both are measured using a respirometer
Wavelengths that are reflected give the highest rates
Light must be absorbed by pigments to be used in photosynthesis
Pigments produce light at the wavelengths they absorb
questions.explanation: Only absorbed light excites electrons, so wavelengths absorbed most strongly (red and blue) give the highest photosynthesis rates; little photosynthesis occurs in green light.

questions.prompt: What is meant by a limiting factor in photosynthesis?
options: The factor that is present in the largest amount
The factor furthest from its optimum, which restricts the rate
Any factor that inhibits enzymes
The product that accumulates fastest
questions.explanation: When several factors affect a process, the rate is limited by the one in shortest supply relative to need. Increasing it raises the rate; increasing other factors does not.

questions.statement: In very dim light, increasing the carbon dioxide concentration greatly increases the rate of photosynthesis.
questions.explanation: In dim light, light intensity is the limiting factor, so extra CO2 has little effect until light intensity is increased.

questions.prompt: The rate of photosynthesis levels off as light intensity increases. Which change would most likely increase the rate further?
options: Increasing light intensity even more
Using green light instead of white light
Removing carbon dioxide
Increasing carbon dioxide concentration
questions.explanation: On the plateau, light is no longer limiting; another factor such as CO2 concentration (or temperature) is, so raising it increases the rate.

questions.text: The rate of photosynthesis in an aquatic plant can be estimated by counting bubbles of ___ released per minute.
questions.explanation: Oxygen is released from photolysis, so the rate of O2 production (bubbles or volume per minute) indicates the rate of photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: How can carbon dioxide concentration be varied in an experiment using pondweed?
options: By adding different concentrations of sodium hydrogencarbonate to the water
By moving a lamp closer to the plant
By placing the plant in a water bath
By using coloured filters
questions.explanation: Sodium hydrogencarbonate releases CO2 in water, so different concentrations give different CO2 levels. Lamp distance varies light intensity; water baths vary temperature.

questions.statement: Above an optimum temperature, the rate of photosynthesis falls because enzymes involved begin to denature.
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis depends on enzymes, so rate rises with temperature up to an optimum and then falls as enzymes denature.

questions.prompt: Match each independent variable to a way of varying it.

pairs.right: Change the distance between lamp and plant
Use different concentrations of sodium hydrogencarbonate

questions.explanation: Each factor can be varied independently while the others are kept constant, so its effect as a limiting factor can be tested.

questions.prompt: What is an advantage of FACE experiments over enclosed greenhouse experiments?
options: They allow light intensity to be controlled precisely
They remove all other limiting factors
Plants grow in natural ecosystems, so predictions of future growth are more realistic
They use lower CO2 concentrations than today
questions.explanation: FACE raises CO2 around plants in the open, so other conditions are natural; greenhouse experiments allow more control but are less like real ecosystems.

questions.text: FACE stands for free-air carbon dioxide ___.
questions.explanation: In free-air CO2 enrichment experiments, CO2 is released over plots of vegetation to predict how rising atmospheric CO2 will affect photosynthesis and plant growth.

questions.prompt: When investigating the effect of light intensity using a lamp, why should a heat shield or LED lamp be used?
options: To increase the light intensity
To keep temperature constant as a controlled variable
To filter out green light
To increase carbon dioxide concentration
questions.explanation: A hot lamp moved closer would also raise temperature, so two variables would change at once. Keeping temperature constant makes it a fair test.

lessons.title: Light-dependent reactions and the Calvin cycle

questions.prompt: What is a photosystem?
options: An array of pigment molecules in a membrane that passes energy to a reaction centre, which emits an excited electron
A single chlorophyll molecule in the stroma
An enzyme that fixes carbon dioxide
A vesicle that stores ATP
questions.explanation: Photosystems are found in thylakoid membranes (and in cyanobacteria). Many pigments absorb light and channel energy to a special chlorophyll pair at the reaction centre.

questions.statement: A single isolated chlorophyll molecule can carry out photosynthesis on its own.
questions.explanation: A structured array of different pigments absorbs a wider range of wavelengths and funnels energy to the reaction centre; a lone pigment molecule cannot perform any part of photosynthesis.

questions.text: Photolysis of water, releasing oxygen, takes place in photosystem ___.
questions.explanation: Photolysis in PSII replaces electrons lost from its reaction centre; protons add to the gradient, and oxygen is released as a waste product.

questions.prompt: How is NADP reduced in the light-dependent reactions?
options: By electrons from photosystem II and protons from the thylakoid space
By ATP from chemiosmosis
By two excited electrons from photosystem I and a proton from the stroma
By oxygen from photolysis
questions.explanation: Excited electrons from PSI are passed to NADP, which also takes up a proton from the stroma, forming reduced NADP for the Calvin cycle.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of non-cyclic photophosphorylation in order.
items: Light excites electrons in the reaction centre of photosystem II
Electrons are replaced by photolysis of water
Electrons pass along carriers and protons are pumped into the thylakoid space
Electrons are re-excited by light in photosystem I
Electrons reduce NADP in the stroma
questions.explanation: Electron flow from PSII to PSI builds a proton gradient used to make ATP by chemiosmosis, and PSI's electrons end up reducing NADP.

questions.prompt: What is produced by cyclic photophosphorylation?
options: ATP, reduced NADP and oxygen
Reduced NADP only
Oxygen and ATP
ATP only
questions.explanation: In cyclic photophosphorylation, excited electrons from PSI return to the electron carriers and back to PSI, pumping protons to make ATP; no NADP is reduced and no water is split.

questions.text: The enzyme that fixes carbon dioxide by combining it with RuBP is ___.
questions.explanation: Rubisco is slow, so chloroplasts have very high concentrations of it in the stroma; it is the most abundant enzyme on Earth.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of the Calvin cycle in order.
items: Two molecules of glycerate 3-phosphate are formed
Glycerate 3-phosphate is reduced to triose phosphate using reduced NADP and ATP
Some triose phosphate is used to make glucose and other compounds
Remaining triose phosphate regenerates RuBP using ATP
questions.explanation: Carbon fixation, reduction and regeneration repeat in a cycle. Triose phosphate also supplies carbon for amino acids and other compounds when mineral nutrients such as nitrogen are available.

questions.prompt: Match each molecule to its role in the Calvin cycle.

pairs.right: 5-carbon CO2 acceptor regenerated by the cycle
3C sugar formed using ATP and reduced NADP

questions.explanation: RuBP + CO2 → 2 GP (catalysed by rubisco); GP is reduced to TP, most of which regenerates RuBP.

questions.statement: In darkness the Calvin cycle soon stops because ATP and reduced NADP are no longer supplied by the light-dependent reactions.
questions.explanation: The two stages are interdependent: the Calvin cycle needs ATP and reduced NADP, and the light-dependent reactions need ADP and NADP returned by the Calvin cycle.

questions.prompt: If glucose is the product, how many out of every 6 triose phosphate molecules are used to regenerate RuBP?
questions.explanation: Five-sixths of triose phosphate is recycled: five TP (15 carbons) regenerate three RuBP (15 carbons). Only one TP in six is a net gain.

questions.prompt: During photophosphorylation, where do protons accumulate before flowing through ATP synthase?
options: In the stroma
In the thylakoid space (lumen)
Between the inner and outer chloroplast membranes
In the cytoplasm
questions.explanation: Electron flow pumps protons into the thylakoid space; they diffuse back into the stroma through ATP synthase, so ATP is made in the stroma where the Calvin cycle uses it.
